hints: Work backwards from Z, think about what type of carbonyl compound gives a positive result with both test reagents.
A positive Tollens test means Z must be an aldehyde, not a ketone, so ask yourself which class of alcohol oxidises to an aldehyde.
Only a primary alcohol gives an aldehyde on mild oxidation, so check which of the four alcohols is primary.
walkthrough:
**Identify what Z must be**

Think about what the two tests tell you. 2,4-DNPH gives an orange precipitate with any carbonyl, so Z is an aldehyde or a ketone.

Test rule: $\text{2,4-DNPH positive} = \text{C=O present}$

**Use Tollens to narrow it down**

Tollens reagent is the decider here. It oxidises aldehydes to give a silver mirror, but ketones do not react.

Test rule: $\text{Tollens positive} = \text{aldehyde, R-CHO}$

So Z must be an aldehyde.

**Link aldehyde back to alcohol Y**

Now recall the oxidation pattern. It is like a family tree and it is worth memorising.

$$\text{primary alcohol} \xrightarrow{[O], mild} \text{aldehyde} \xrightarrow{[O]} \text{carboxylic acid}$$
$$\text{secondary alcohol} \xrightarrow{[O]} \text{ketone (no further oxidation)}$$
$$\text{tertiary alcohol} \xrightarrow{[O]} \text{no reaction}$$

Since Z is an aldehyde, Y must be a primary alcohol.

**Check the four alcohols**

Butan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, has the $\text{-OH}$ on a carbon with two H atoms, so it is primary. It oxidises mildly to butanal, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, which fits both tests perfectly.

options.A: Butan-1-ol is a primary alcohol. Mild oxidation gives butanal, an aldehyde. Butanal has a C=O group so gives orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH, and as an aldehyde it reduces Tollens reagent to give the silver mirror. This matches Z exactly.
options.B: Butan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Oxidation gives butanone, a ketone. Ketones give a positive 2,4-DNPH test but a negative Tollens test, so this cannot be Z.
options.C: Butan-2,3-diol contains two secondary alcohol groups. Oxidation would give carbonyls at those positions, leading to ketone type products (like butane-2,3-dione), not a simple aldehyde. These would be 2,4-DNPH positive but Tollens negative. A common trap is to think two OH groups means an aldehyde must form.
options.D: 2-methylbutan-2-ol is a tertiary alcohol. The carbon bearing the OH has no H atoms to remove, so it resists mild oxidation and no product Z would form. Students sometimes forget to check the alcohol class first.
